newsitem.title: USA: INSTANT VIEW - US Jan trade gap totals $12.71 bln.
newsitem.headline: INSTANT VIEW - US Jan trade gap totals $12.71 bln.

text.p: Following are comments from economists after the Commerce Department reported the January international trade gap at $12.71 billion compared to a upwardly revised $10.49 billion deficit in December.
Economists in a Reuters survey had expected a $10.7 billion gap in the latest month.
ADAM CHESTER, INTERNATIONAL TRADE ANALYST, YAMAICHI INTERNATIONAL (LONDON): "I think it's clearly a surprising figure.

"(The figures) do highlight the fact that the improvement that we saw in the trade balance in the U.S. in the fourth quarter has come to a startling halt. The results of that, I imagine, is that analysts will now be revising down their first quarter GDP forecast."

DAVID SLOAN, ECONOMIST, I.D.E.A. INC: "It's obviously a bad figure, mainly imports seem to be the problem. It seems to me the biggest problems are with China and Mexico. The deficits with Japan and Western Europe weren't such a bad thing.
"Exports are weak, although most of the decline in exports were probably related to aircraft.
"It's certainly a disappointing figure. It will subtract from (first quarter) GDP, although Q1 GDP should be fairly strong through good consumer spending.
"The strong rise in imports is a response to stronger consumer spending in the U.S."
RICHARD BERNER, CHIEF ECONOMIST, MELLON BANK CORP: "Remember that we had some bad weather in January that probably inhibited export shipments more than imports.
"There's a second factor: Exports were exaggerated on the strong side in the fourth quarter (and) we're getting some payback for that in the first quarter.
"Obviously, strong domestic demand in the U.S. is resulting in stronger imports.

"We're going to see a widening of the trade gap in the first quarter. This confirms that. The issue going forward is, as overseas economic strength picks up, will it boost U.S. exports. I think the answer to that is yes."

ASTRID ADOLFSON, FIRST VICE PRESIDENT AND ECONOMIST, MCM MONEYWATCH INC: "(The data) do show consensus ... the imports rose, which is in line with stronger growth here versus the weaker growth overseas."
"The Treasury bond market is focusing on (Federal Reserve Chairman Alan) Greenspan ... I don't think these (data) matter as much."
STEVEN WIETING, ASSOCIATE ECONOMIST, SMITH BARNEY INC.: "Trade will be a large subtraction to first quarter growth, undoing what it did to growth in the fourth quarter.
"We're looking for 2.7 percent growth in the first quarter ... For 1997, we expect trade to be a big drag on economic growth."

SANDY BATTEN, INTERNATIONAL ECONOMIST, CITICORP GLOBAL FINANCE: "Exports were as we expected. A decline in aircraft exports more than accounted for all the export fall in the month. On the import side, there were small increases across the board but there was a substantial increase in auto imports. That reflects a stronger dollar and increased auto exports from Japan.

"It means that some of the sales strength we saw in January was produced abroad. That means more growth related to strong demand is leaking out to production abroad. When you see these demand figures, you have to figure out where the stuff is being produced.

"We're going to have pretty decent GDP growth in the first quarter, but according to these data, which of course are just for the first month of the quarter, it's not going to be elevated to the extent that last week's retail sales figures might have led you to believe."
(( N.A. Treasury Desk, 212-859-1660 ))
